question: What historical freshwater fish catch evidence does the 2013 Paghungawan Marsh report provide, and what can safely be attributed to the named Siargao marsh sites?

study.title: Status of Introduced Philippine Crocodiles (Crocodylus mindorensis) in Paghongawan Marsh, Siargao Island, Philippines
study.publication: Crocodile Specialist Group Newsletter, IUCN Species Survival Commission, 32(3), 20-22 (July-September 2013).
study.recordType: Field-project report in a specialist newsletter; fishery assessment is a component of a crocodile-release and marsh-productivity monitoring study.
study.access: The full newsletter PDF was read from a publicly accessible mirror. No account, payment, author contact or access-control bypass was used.
study.reuse: No item-specific reuse license was located in the reviewed issue. Public availability is not treated as permission to reproduce the fish list, counts, photographs or page content in the app.

followupCrossCheck.citation: Bucol, A. A., Manalo, R. I., Alcala, A. C., & Aspilla, P. S. (2020). Crocodilians and fisheries in the Philippines: revisiting Fittkau's hypothesis. Philippine Journal of Systematic Biology, 14(2), 1-9. https://doi.org/10.26757/pjsb2020b14004
followupCrossCheck.reportedMethod: The paper reports fishery sampling with three 15 m x 1.5 m gillnets of 1.5 cm mesh, one hour per net, and says fish were identified using standard references. It dates Paghungawan gillnetting to 8 June 2013 and 9 October 2014.
followupCrossCheck.reconciliation: The 2020 paper's June 2013 length-analysis N for O. niloticus (82) differs from the 2013 newsletter's fishery-composition count (199). The papers do not explain whether the length N is a measured subsample or otherwise reconcile the counts. Preserve both as source-specific values; do not combine them or derive abundance, trend, catch rate or relative abundance from the difference.
followupCrossCheck.historicalProtectionContext: The 2020 paper reports a 2013 barangay gillnet/poison-substance prohibition and a PAMB strict-protection classification. This review does not verify current legal text, boundaries, exceptions or status; no fishing-rule claim is admitted.

interpretation.safeSummary: The 2013 field-project report documents source-reported fishery samples from two named freshwater-marsh areas in Siargao: six labels and 245 fish at Paghongawan, and four labels and 98 fish for the San Mateo/Sangay-Lilaw comparison area. One Paghongawan label is only Anguilla cf. marmorata, not a confirmed species identification. The report gives no museum vouchers, individual capture coordinates, station-by-taxon matrix, complete seasonal inventory or current survey.
scopeBoundaries: This is a historical, gear-selective fishery sample, not a complete freshwater fish inventory or a current-presence assessment.
Catch counts do not measure population size or abundance; effort, gear selectivity, site pooling and later count reconciliation limit comparison.
The source's possible crocodile prey observations are not fish stomach-content evidence and do not establish natural diet for any fish species.
The San Mateo list is not separable into the two ponds named Sangay and Lilaw.
No marsh polygon or waterbody boundary can be inferred from a study-site coordinate.
The later paper's reported 2013 prohibition is historical context, not current legal guidance.
notSupported: A current or complete species list for either marsh.
Confirmed Anguilla marmorata at Paghungawan Marsh.
Per-pond or station-level species assignments, a marsh geometry, or a collection/voucher record.
Natural diet, bait suggestions, fish safety, present abundance, or current legal catchability.

disposition.reason: The newsletter provides valuable historical catch leads, but the study is not a complete inventory, voucher links are absent, one identification is qualified cf., later same-program sample Ns are not reconciled, and app reuse rights are unverified.

references.supports: 2013 field-report title/authors/pages, study period and sites, reported Paghongawan and San Mateo fish counts and source names, and the report's own limits/context.
Follow-up study site names/coordinates, salinity classification, gillnet methods and dates, reported length-analysis sample sizes, and its retrospective protection-context statement.
Persistent identifier for the 2020 follow-up article.

nextAction: Continue the Caraga inland-water sweep with a separate accessible primary fish survey or specimen-backed source from a distinct named river, lake or marsh. Keep the Paghungawan and Sangay-Lilaw catch evidence historical and research-only; do not infer absence from a missing index record.
